text.p: The International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday that Moldova's economic peformance was not satisfactory and payments of a $195 million loan would continue to be delayed unless there was an improvement.
A statement issued in advance of the arrival next week of an IMF mission said the former Soviet republic had agreed measures to improve performance with an earlier mission in February.

If Moldova carries out these steps, and agrees a programme for the rest of the year with the new mission, the fund's board may agree at its meeting in July to resume payments, IMF resident representative Mark Horton said.
"But that is not a sure thing. Implementation of the agreed package of measures is relatively positive, but the mission and the IMF board have to make the final decision", he told Reuters.

The new mission, visiting from April 14 to 25, will review progress on the measures agreed in Feburary. It has a long list of economic problems to discuss with Moldova, a small, largely agricultural country lying between Romania and Ukraine.
As with many other former Soviet republics, key issues are the size of the budget deficit and the level of tax revenues, and unpaid wages and pensions.
These now total about $150 million, while Moldova, largely dependent on Russia for energy, owes Russian gas monopoly Gazprom some $570 million.
The IMF is also concerned that Moldova has not yet approved a privatisation programme for 1997 and 1998.
Many of these problems surfaced in the middle of last year.

"Moldova's performance... was not fully satisfactory in the third and fourth quarters of 1996, reflecting mainly a deterioration of the budget deficit, worsening pension and wage arrears and continuing difficulties in the energy sector", the IMF statement said.

Until early last year the fund had been full of guarded praise for Moldova's economic reforms, which have seen the new leu currency stabilise and inflation come down, despite a steep recession which has kept many people in poverty.
The economy is now barely one third of its size in 1989, and has fallen back to levels last seen in 1966.
The fund agreed the $195 million three-year Extended Fund Facility in May 1996, paying out two tranches of $16.25 million each in May and July.
But the fund has delayed the two tranches due in the third and fourth quarters of last year.
Other donors have also become more cautious.

James Parks, the World Bank's representative in Moldova, said the Moldovan economy was causing serious concern because of the slower pace of structural reforms after an initial successful period of stabilisation.
Annual inflation slowed to 15.1 percent in 1996, keeping the currency stable, while foreign exchange reserves rose to $315 million.

But gross domestic product continued to fall, shrinking about eight percent in 1996, while the budget deficit came in at eight percent of GDP instead of the planned 3.5 percent. This year's budget deficit is targeted at three percent of GDP.

The World Bank says it is ready to grant Moldova a structural adjustment loan to help reforms, which will be at least $60 million, but first wants to see evidence of political will to push ahead with economic reforms.

"We have developed a very detailed reform programme for Moldova. Political decision is needed to implement it. At the moment it is taken, the credit will be available," Hafez Ghanem of the World Bank said in March. andquot
